subject: How to model scale of beta distribtuion

messages.author: 06b57f25e554a736
messages.subject: How to model scale of beta distribtuion
parts:
I'm currently modeling a proportion as a beta distribution where the mean is inv_logit(a linear function of the features). The features are multiple continuous variables and several sets of dummy categorical variables. Currently the scale of the beta distribution is a global parameter, i.e. independent of the features. That model is after his email ("Global scale model").

My question is: is there a "usual" or "right" way to extend this model so that lambda, the scale of the beta distribution, is also a function of the features? At the moment I'm just taking the exponential (to ensure strictly positive) of a linear combination of the features. This works in the sense that if compiles and runs, but the results look a little off to me, and I suspect that my data is poorly described by this model. I realize the right thing to do will depend strongly on the data, but I'm wondering if anyone can point me towards some common approaches to this problem? "Varying scale model" below is what I have at the moment.

I mentioned that I'm modeling a proportion in case that makes a difference, and if there are better/different approaches to this particular problem then I'm all ears! But I think perhaps this is a generic problem of modeling the scale of a distribution, i.e. it's equivalent to the situation where the sd of a normal distribution depends on the same features as the mean.

Mike

# Global scale model

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> K; // Number of features
matrix[N, K] X;
vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] proportion;
}
parameters {
vector[N_features] phi_coef;
real lambda; // lambda of beta distribution = a + b
}
model {
vector[N] Xphi
vector[N] phi; // mean of beta distribution = a/(a+b)
vector[N] a;
vector[N] b;

Xphi <- X_unpaid * phi_coef;
for (i in 1:N_unpaid) {
phi[i] <- inv_logit(Xphi[i]);
}
a <- phi * lambda;
b <- lambda * (1 - phi);

lambda ~ pareto(0.1,1.5)
phi_coef ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
proportion ~ beta(a, b);
}

# Varying scale model

parameters {
vector[N_features] phi_coef;
vector[N_features] lambda_coef;
}
model {
vector[N] Xphi;
vector[N] lambda;
vector[N] phi; // mean of beta distribution = a/(a+b)
vector[N] lambda; // lambda of beta distribution = a+b
vector[N] a;
vector[N] b;

Xphi_coef <- X_unpaid * phi;
Xlambda_coef <- X_unpaid * lambda;
for (i in 1:N) {
phi[i] <- inv_logit(Xphi[i]); // between 0 and 1
lambda[i] <- exp(Xlambda[i]); // between 0 and +infinity
}
a <- phi .* lambda;
b <- lambda .* (1 - phi);

phi_coef ~ cauchy(0, 2.5;
lambda_coef[1] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
proportion ~ beta(a, b);
}

On Monday, July 11, 2016 at 8:47:59 PM UTC-4, Michael Williams wrote:
My question is: is there a "usual" or "right" way to extend this model so that lambda, the scale of the beta distribution, is also a function of the features? At the moment I'm just taking the exponential (to ensure strictly positive) of a linear combination of the features. This works in the sense that if compiles and runs, but the results look a little off to me, and I suspect that my data is poorly described by this model. I realize the right thing to do will depend strongly on the data, but I'm wondering if anyone can point me towards some common approaches to this problem? "Varying scale model" below is what I have at the moment.

My guess is the model runs into problems when the non-mean parameter (it is not really a scale parameter) gets to be less than 1, in which case you get these U-shaped beta distributions that presumably do not correspond to your beliefs about the outcomes. One way to overcome this is to shift it over by 1 as in

model {
  vector[N] mu;
  vector[N] lambda;
  mu = inv_logit(X * mu_coef);
  lambda = 1 + exp(X * lambda_coef);
  target += beta_lpdf(y | mu .* lambda, (1 - mu) .* lambda);
  ...
}

Ben
